title: Rent Control Board Candidates Forum
description: Videos provided to you by the City of Santa Monica.

[music] [music] >> [music] >> You ready to get started [music] when everyone Good evening and welcome to the 2026 Santa Monica Rent Control Board Candidate Forum. My name is September Ray and I'm with the League of Women Voters of Santa Monica Education Fund who along with the City of Santa Monica is co-sponsoring this forum. Both co-sponsoring groups are nonpartisan nonprofit organizations, which means that they do not support or oppose candidates for public office. For more information about the League of Women Voters Education Fund, please check out the information table in the back of the room. My task as moderator this evening is to present questions to the candidates and to provide a civil and productive environment by graciously but firmly enforcing the guidelines and rules that were agreed to by all candidates. Before we go over go any further, I'd like to go over a few ground rules. First, as a matter of courtesy, we ask that everyone, including the audience, please turn off their phones. Second, to maintain the neutrality of this forum, campaign literature and other forms of campaigning such as buttons, t-shirts, and signs are not permitted inside the forum room. Also, audience members are expected to refrain from interjecting, including clapping, shouting, cheering, groaning, or stomping during the forum and particularly when anyone is speaking. Candidates, we also ask that you refrain from personally addressing or attacking other candidates and instead focus on letting voters know why you believe you are best qualified to serve as a member of the Santa Monica Rent Control Board. This year, there are three open seats for the Santa Monica Rent Control Board. All candidates who are qualified and are running for this office have been invited to participate. Each candidate participating in tonight's forum will have the opportunity to answer a variety of questions. I will be be presenting these questions to the candidates in random order. The candidates will have between 1 and 1 and 1/2 minutes to answer as noted by me. Candidates sitting in the front row are our timers. Timers, please raise the paddles. Candidates, you'll see time on the paddle indicates how much time you have left to answer a question. When you see the stop sign, please finish your sentence. We'll turn to our first question. Candidates, you'll have one minute to respond. Please start by stating your name and telling us why you are running for a seat on the Santa Monica Rent Control Board. Sue Himmorich, you will have the floor first. Thank you. And thank you, September. Thank you, League of Women Voters. Thank you, City of Santa Monica for hosting this forum. And I do really hope that in the future we can arrange to do it on something other than a Friday night. Uh uh I'm Sue Himmel Rich and I'm running for rent board because I don't just talk about protecting tenants. I've spent the last 20 years fighting for them. As a public interest attorney, I've stood in courtrooms defending renters against displacement. As your council member and mayor, I didn't just vote for affordable housing and tenant protections. I fought for them budget line by budget line, meeting by meeting, tenant by tenant. As your neighbor, I had I led campaigns to pass both 2016 and 2022 measures GS, which finance ongoing and emergency income support for at risk renters, lawyers for renters facing eviction, and the creation of affordable housing units. I walk the talk because when landlords push back on protections, I don't fold. I push back harder. Thank you for your time. >> Thank you, Zoe Montaner. You'll have the floor next. >> Good evening. My name is So Monteneer. I am a resident of Santa Monica since 1998. I moved here from Puerto Rico. I moved to New York in 2005 and I returned to Santa Monica in 2010 because this is home. My parents um passed and we sold the property in Puerto Rico. So this is my home now and my community. I'm the founder of Compassionate Santa Monica and Giving Tuesday Santa Monica. And I have faced numerous instances of tenant harassment and unlawful evictions and the lack of protections from the city of Santa Monica that takes great pride in being a city of renters that protect renters. But the reality is that when you knock on the doors of the rent control board and the city attorney office and code enforcement, I've been faced with multiple and multiple closed doors and ignorance of the facts. Thank you. >> Thank you, Heather Thomasson. You have the floor. >> Hi, thank you so much for having us tonight. My name is Heather Thomasson and I'm running for the rent control board in Santa Monica because I strongly believe in rent control. I have personally lived the difference that it makes. Um I was a renter for 16 years before I became a homeowner and eight of those years were in rent controlled a rent controlled unit. um which I came to very intentionally after I was displaced multiple times in um non-controlled units where my rent was raised 50% in one year. Another unit I moved into, I was forced to leave after a year because the landlord was selling. I believe that it is one of the greatest assets of this community that gives us our greatest chance at socioeconomic diversity being preserved. Um, and I see that there are more threats than ever to rent control right now. Um, partly because of the state housing laws that don't protect it well enough and I'd like to be here to protect it. Thank you. >> Thank you. Kurt Ganska, you have the floor. >> Hi everybody. My name is Kurt Ganska and thank you to the League of Women Voters and Santa Monica for hosting tonight. I've been a commissioner on the Santa Monica Rank Control Board since 2022. I served as board chair last year and I'm running for reelection because I'm proud of the hard work that I put in and the accomplishments in my first term on the board. I served on two important subcommittees. One that resulted in increasing how much tenants can receive in rent decreases. The other uh develop charter amendments that are on the ballot this November before voters. I also helped ban algorithmic price fixing software, supported capping mark hetup rent increases, and worked with my fellow commissioners to hire a new executive director and general counsel. I'm endorsed by the Santa Monicans for renters rights, Santa Monica Democratic Club, Los Angeles County Democratic Party, Westside Young Dems, Unite Here, and others. Uh, as well as a bunch of community leaders like the um, Smur co-chairs Denny Zayn and Mike Solaf, and former rent control executive director Tracy Condan. So, I hope to earn your support as well tonight. Thank you. >> Thank you, Soladad Marisal. >> Hi, my name is Soladad Martial. I've been a renter since the 80s in the Pico neighborhood. I went to school here. I went to Will Rogers Elementary School all the way through Santa Monica College. And that gives me the understanding of the challenges that we face. Santa Monicans rely on rent control to stay housed. For years, I've helped many of my neighbors, especially those who are afraid to speak up and address issues of ignore repairs, uncashed rental checks, and threats of evictions. Through my lived experience, I've earned their trust and the necessary connections for tenants to connect the tenants with the right resources. And I would like to continue doing that if I'm elected. Thank you. >> Thank you. For our next question, you will all have one minute to respond. Please tell us in what area of Santa Monica you live, whether you rent or own your home, and whether you have ever been a renter or a landlord in the city, and then please explain how your experiences will shape your perspective as a board member. Kurt, you will have the floor first. >> Okay, I'll try to remember. If I missed any of those, please let me know. But >> happy to repeat the question at any time. >> I'll give it a shot first. Um, I live uh on Third in Washington in Wilmont. uh and uh I've been there uh in a rent control department since 2019. Before that, I was on Sanenti uh in a rent control department. So, I've been in Santa Monica since 2014. And before that, I grew up in and went to school in Chicago and then moved straight to Santa Monica. It's the only place I've lived in LA and I love it here and want to stay here forever. Um and what was the second part? >> How will these experiences shape your work? >> I need a lot more time to explain that. Hopefully I'll have an opportunity uh later in this forum. But uh I came to the rent control board initially because of a problem with my landlord in my rent control department. And through that process, I learned all about the what we have here, the amazing rights, the amazing uh charter amen charter that we have, the amazing rent control staff that we have and went through a whole process with my issue personally and learned how I can help others the same way that they helped me. >> Thank you. Soladad, you have the floor. Um, like I said in my previous answer, I've lived here since the 80s and um, I lived in the Pico neighborhood all the time. There was a time when I was outpriced from Santa Monica and moved for a little while to South Central LA. Um, through my work, I happened to come back to Santa Monica and that's how I ended up in a rent control apartment back in 2018. And, uh, I raised my kids here. Um I mean half of my family is here as well and how the you said how it changed my experience the second >> how does it shape your experience? Well, I love Santa Monica, but I would like Santa Monica to go back to being community oriented because even though back in the 80s we were growing up with like gangs in the neighborhood, we still had that community feeling. We would we would know all the kids around. We would all walk to school together. Thank you. >> Thank you, Zoe. You have the floor. >> Hi. [clears throat] Hello. >> Have Yes. Uh I live >> Okay. I live on Seventh Street um right now behind Samo High. Before that, I live at 643 Pacific. That is in Ocean Park. I have lived in multiple neighborhoods. I've lived in Wilmont on 113114th Street and I have lived in north of Montana. So, I know the city uh very well and I can see that each neighborhood has its own personality and its own challenges and its own blessings. Um, currently I'm in a position to really speak about tenant harassment because I moved to with a roommate. a lot of people have been a um to stay in Santa Monica, moved to with roommates and he ended up sexually harassing me. Um and that finally he left the apartment and he vacated the apartment. But now I'm facing you know an issue with the landlord and I faced um numerous challenges with my downstairs neighbor that is actually here trying to harass me and he's sitting sitting in the audience. We ask that all candidates remember the guidelines that ask that we don't call out people. Thank you. Sue, you have the floor. >> Thank you. Um I've lived in Santa Monica maybe longer than people on this dis have been have lived altogether. I moved to Santa Monica in 1992. Uh live I moved to LA in 1983. I was a renter for a short time. I was one of those brave women who bought a home before women could get credit. I'm proud of that. And I've never been ashamed of being a homeowner. And I'm a homeowner now with my husband, but I own my home before he ever owned a home. And we bought it together. And uh uh what really brought me to this is being a lawyer. I've defended tenants. I worked for Western Center on Law and Poverty. I've uh uh I became involved in Santa Monica through something called Village Trailer Park where a bunch of seniors were evicted to make way for a development. We still have 10 trailers there. But basically, I come at this from a lawyer's perspective and believe that tenant rights should be uh uh respected and protected. >> Thank you, Heather. You have the floor. >> Thank you. Um I am currently a homeowner. I have been living in Santa Monica for four years. Before that, I lived in Venice for 15. Um, and I had um a rent controlled apartment that was a huge gift to my life. Um, it brought me stability that I hadn't had before. It really changed my life. It allowed me to feel secure in where I was and um like I could take a chance on starting a family because I wouldn't be uprooted in the middle of everything. Um it also allowed me to plan for the future and and save in a way that helped me actually um get to [clears throat] a place where I could buy my house which I you know own with the bank mostly. Um, and I will say that one of the experiences that was really important for me that I think guides some of how I think about this is that I had an a wonderful relationship with my landlord. I know not everybody does, but I actually did and I I recognize the importance of that sort of relationship and um that it's a symbiotic one for all of us. Thanks. Thank you. For the next question, you all have one minute to respond. What will be your first priority if elected on the rent control board and how do you intend to accomplish it? Soladad, you'll have the floor first. My first priority would be uh extending public outreach and the reason for that um I've been that's one of my ma major issues but also yesterday I heard uh a tenant also bring this up and the rent control board saying how now because it's election season he gets tons of flyers on in the mail, but that doesn't happen on a regular basis for outreach so that they know their rights and responsibilities. So, that's my one priority. Thank you. >> Thank you, Heather. You have the floor. Um I think one of the greatest programs that we have right now is the small debt rental relief program um that was funded by measure GS and um I am very interested in uh if measure RR passes um to be able to especially I mean I'm interested in it either way but I I I'm I'm really hopeful that that will because I think that that will give us time to reach tenants who need assistance when they are on the verge of eviction. Right now, the rent control board doesn't receive information. Um it's not a requirement to receive information about um uh rental debt based evictions. And if we can kind of bring those things together um under the one roof, that would be a priority because nobody should be um losing their apartments over small rental debt. >> Thank you. Kurt, you have the floor. One of the things um that I want to work on uh in the second term is modernizing some of the rent control agencies um the public facing technology. So one example is um the way that uh the forms and the process for submitting a rent decrease petition. Um it's I think probably a process and the the forms have been used for many many years and I think that there are ways that could make it easier for uh tenants because the the rent decrease process for both landlords and tenants can be quite complex and um lengthy. So anything we can do up front to make it easier to submit those uh petitions, the supporting documents, the evidence, all of that electronically um would be I think a big help for tenants. So, I want to I want to work with the staff to uh implement some changes there. >> Thank you. Sue, you have the floor. >> Wait a minute. Let's try that again. My mic is on. Uh first, I want to say that I appreciate what all of you said and I agree with everything you said. I think that those are all important issues. Um I am a lawyer. I believe in code enforcement. I think that we have habitability issues in many of our units. Let me just say that once you're off the council or you aren't the mayor anymore, you don't stop hearing about people's issues in their apartments and their habitability issues and their problems with the rent control board. I still hear those things and I do hear most frequently about habitability issues. I believe that there's a way that we can bring code enforcement um uh under the city attorney's office and that we can begin to enforce many of our regulations that we don't enforce uh primarily through um other means of financing. They're already doing this in other jurisdictions. That would be my major goal to begin with, but again, I agree with everything the rest of you said and so I would support you fully in any of those. >> Thank you, Zoe. I also agree with everybody everything, but I came to the rent control board meeting yesterday and I actually spoke about a conversation that I had with Brian Goldmith that hopefully becomes our next senator. And [clears throat] I'm really focusing on the sustainability department partnering with energy efficient um replacement of windows AC and as we know you know we live in California and we have mandatory heating system but we don't have mandatory AC and with the issue of global warming and the heat that we are experiencing um working with Brian to see if he can pass legislation in California to make this mandatory. And for the property owners, we need to get rebates so we can stimulate that uh upgrades of habitability and especially AC for um elderly people that are disabled and cannot leave their apartments. These uh heat problems can create heat strokes and people die. and we have a president in Florida. Thank you. >> Thank you. >> Following up on that, climate change is upon us. You will all have one minute to respond to this question. In August 2025, LA County passed the safe indoor temperature ordinance requiring landlords to keep habitable rooms at or below 82° F. Santa Monica hasn't explored opting in. This summer, and specifically in the last week, renters in older Santa Monica buildings without AC, including seniors and families with small children, regularly experienced indoor temperatures exceeding the 82° threshold. What can you do to encourage the adoption of this ordinance and others like it to protect renters and others? Sue, you have the floor first. Well, I would certainly support something like that, although frankly, I'm not sure that's within the jurisdiction of the rent control board. I mean, it's a great question, but frankly, I think that that is a legislative issue that falls within the purview of the city council, and I am pretty mindful of the guard rails that are on the rent control board to keep us in the rent control arena. Uh although 70% of the people in the city are renters, it doesn't mean that 70% of the apartments are rent controlled apartments. So, I think that there needs to be a wider uh mandate that um relates to more than simply rent control when it comes to this, but again, I think that it's a worthwhile question and given global warming, we need to answer it. Thank you. >> Thank you. Zoe, you have the floor. >> As I said before, um I was in a meeting on Thursday. a woman that lived in Florida uh told me about the numbers of heat stroke victims um and the majority were elderly and disabled because of the heat in Florida. And I agree with Sue that is not in the purview, but that's why we need to build relationships with Sacramento and with the city council to pass legislation that actually helps the rent control give that service. We have high rents and our amenities should reflect uh apartments that have the amenities that the rent that we are paying is worth and you know it is something that I'm passionate about because this is how a lot of people get placed out because they cannot live in a place that they are not supported anymore. Thank you. Thank you. Heather, you have the floor. >> Um, I will say that um though it may not be in our in our purview, um, as somebody who has been going through the campaign to be a rent control board member, I've been hearing from a lot of community members and there is definitely appetite from the community for this and rent controlled units. Um, and so I think that, you know, one of the things that we should kind of obviously do is reach out to the tenants to find out how important of an issue is this to many of them. And um one thing that I do think that we have to be careful with as we pursue it or the city council pursues it um is that we're not creating a situation where we're going to end up raising rents for tenants um based on having to do this because that's a real risk with something like this. But it's all, you know, it's a delicate balance and we'll have to find the right one because this is real. >> Thank you. Kurt, you have the floor. >> Yeah, I agree with a lot of what's been said so far. Um, I think that I I do support an ordinance. Um, obviously it depends on the exact details, but generally I support the the or related ordinance. And I think if we were to do something like that, it's important that we um have the ability to uh help building owners who may need assistance with the cost for that. Not necessarily everybody. Um, you can develop a system where those who have a need can get help. And that goes for tenants as well because you might have air conditioning under an ordinance like that, but it's going to cost a lot in heat waves to for the electricity to power that air conditioning. So, people may need support on both fronts. Um, but how to get it done is relationships with city council members. Um, I'm endorsed by five city council members, including uh Mayor Terrosus. Um, and I've worked with them on a lot of different issues over the years. So I feel confident I can start those conversations and advocate for it even if we can't do it directly on the rent control board. >> Thank you. Salad. >> I think that everything that's been said is more than I can I can say to um an ordinance like this. I really agree with grants because that's that's what makes the difference and it won't have to raise rents. But um definitely looking into it and um I had one of the uh one of the uh Sunset Park members come up to me as well and talk to me about this and she is very passionate about it. So I would love to work with that person. >> Thank you. >> Thank you. >> For our next question, all candidates will be given 90 seconds to respond. Reading this year's rent control board annual report, it looks like the board is engaged in a tugof-war with the forces of Costa Hawkins and the Ellis Act on one side and city regulations on the other. It doesn't look like a fair game. What would you change and what can you change? Heather, you have the floor first. question. >> Can you read that question again? Didn't make a lot of I'm sorry. >> No, happy to read. I can tell you that you're talking about laws and I want to understand it better. Please. >> Of course. Reading this year's rent control board annual report, it looks like the board is engaged in a tugof-war with the forces of Costa Hawkins and the Ellis Act on one side and the city regulations on the other. It doesn't look like a fair game. What would you change and what can you change? Heather, you still have the mic. >> Okay, thank you. Um, so yeah, I mean I guess what what we're talking about is um buildings, you know, what what we're up against is buildings being taken off the market. Um, and uh and our inability to expand the rental stock um those are really um critical issues for us. And I guess some of the areas that I think about when working sort of within the bounds of the law are I think about advocating with the [clears throat] city council to raise um rates for um tenant relocations um to you know sort of dissuade the removal of units. Um, I think about things like making sure that tenants uh understand how valuable their units really are so that when they're facing buyout offers that they aren't under, you know, they aren't shortch changing themselves. I actually spoke to a person today in a building who had just the building had just sold and um there were people that were already facing long-term tenants that were already facing some harassment. Um and he was telling me that one person had accepted like $10,000 to leave their apartment. And I was stunned and just thinking, "Oh my gosh, what a what a what a gift they just gave up for not enough." Um, so those are some of the areas that I think just sort of dissuading people from taking things off the market and kicking people out. >> Thank you. So, Lad, you have the floor. Um, it helps local government address one of the root causes of homelessness and skyrocketing rents and unaffordable housing. And um, you said there was another part of the question. Sorry. >> What would you change? >> That's what I would change. >> And then what can you change as a rent control board member? >> What can I change? I can work with legislators in order to make this happen. >> Thank you. >> Thank you. >> Sue, you have the floor. >> Thank you. We're constantly striving to keep up with Costa Hawkins and Ellis and make sure that our tenants get the best shot shot under those regulations. Um I I think that um that landlords have a right and it I always say it's their job to make more money and it's our job to say no. So, it's our job to make sure that tenants have as many protections as possible under our laws and under the rubric that's created by the state and that is really governed by um the real estate interests that have more lobbying power than we do and more lobbying power than any city has and more lobbying power uh certainly than most tenants have. Now the people who are living in the apartments in Santa Monica are not those people, not the people that I represent, although some of them are. And it is it is incumbent upon us as rent board commissioners to protect those tenants no matter what happens and that's what I would do. >> Thank you Kurt. You have the floor. >> Thank you. But in some cases it actually works out where tenants are pretty happy to get to go back to a new unit at their existing rent price. Um as it relates to um Costa Hawkins, it's not something within my purview on the rent control board certainly, but I would like to see uh the ability for additional units to become rent controlled, which currently they cannot. So this is and then I heard of elderly disabled men that came to that meeting as well. Um, and I want to open an EDN West here that service not only Santa Monica but the west side of Los Angeles. [clears throat] Kurt, you will have the floor first. >> Yeah, it's certainly true. uh to to pass an a regulation or anything on the rent control board, you need three of the five commissioners. And so that requires um persuasion, but it also requires just a lot of conversation and relationship building with the other commissioners and frankly with the with our executive director, our general counsel um because we rely on them a lot for information and for analysis. So um I think there there are numerous examples over my four years on the board. um the two subcommittees that I mentioned earlier uh where I worked closely with another commissioner initially um that's actually a really good example because when we when we're on subcommittees there are a lot of meetings that occur between the two member the two commissioners who are in the subcommittee um but then we have to bring that information to the full board and bring the other commissioners up to speed and and be persuasive with them to get at least that third vote but hopefully to build a consensus where we're getting unanimous support um and because of the Brown Act we can't then be discussing those topics with the other three commissioners until we're in front of the public in a in a public meeting. So um there have been the two subcommittees specifically but a lot of examples over the years of um working with the other commissioners to to build support for initiatives that I'm supporting. >> Thank you. Zoe, you have the floor. >> Thank you for that question. Um, I remember when I passed um the charter for compassion, I had a unanimous vote from city council in September 24 of 2013. None of us are perfect and we all have different backgrounds and different biases uh implicit or explicit biases. But at this is not about us. This is about the renters of Santa Monica. So, I don't think the new general council is going to foster that environment that we need to work with each other and to work with the residents and the renters of the city. Thank you. >> Thank you, Sue. You have the floor. >> Thank you. Um so in my years on city council um I did work collaboratively with sorry collaboratively with other council members although there have been time there were times where um I had to convince them that my way was the right way. So, for instance, when I was on the uh council, we implemented an audit committee and we did this because we had a civil jur jury grant uh civil grand jury report that said we should do it. Uh every responsible organization with income such as ours, close to a uh a billion dollars a year, was had an audit committee. The idea that our city council was our audit committee was absurd. Now, there was a lot of push back, but ultimately the city council did pass this, and I don't think it was unanimous, but it's been a success. And there have been other programs that have been successes, but part of being in government is being able to talk to other people and be collaborative with other people. Um, I I just believe that it's an important tenant of government that you talk to your constituents, all of your constituents, not just the ones you agree with. Um, and the same with your board members. There are going to be board members you don't agree with and you have to speak to all of them and you have to speak to them civily and you have to speak to them in a way that speaks to them and not in the way that speaks to you. I mean, we always say in the legal profession that what you need to argue. Sorry, you're never going to hear that. Thank you. [laughter] >> There you have the floor. >> Um, yeah. So, I um am a TV writer and a screenwriter in my day job. And in a TV room, we spend all day trying to come to consensus while we all have very different ideas about how things should go in a story. And I find that the best approach to that is curiosity around why people are seeing things the way that they are seeing it. and trying to just really understand um first so that you can take that disagreement on its own terms. Um I also see this in my life as a parent of young children where um trying to force them to do anything is just a failing mission. And so, you know, it's important to try to get buy in from people and do that by understanding what they don't understand about what you're saying. Um, and I I think that all of that is going to serve me really well and apply to the work on this board. Um, and I look forward to working with everybody on it. >> Thank you, Soladad. Hi, I've worked in customer service most of my life and the approach that I've always taken is listening to everyone. Taking into consideration the bigger picture and the people we serve as a whole to come up with the best outcome for the people that we are serving. Not what I feel like. What I feel I know is the emotion at that moment, but if we take a step back and we look at it from a different perspective, then how is that going to serve the community as a whole? Thank you. >> Thank you. That concludes our candidate forum for tonight. On behalf of the League of Women Voters of Santa Monica Education Fund and the City of Santa Monica, we thank all of you for taking part in tonight's candidates forum and for stepping forward to run for office. We also thank all the volunteers who help with tonight's forum. And we thank all of you watching us. Remember, elections are won by the people that vote. >> [music]
